title: How the Model of the Atom Developed
keyIdea: The model of the atom changed each time new evidence did not fit. Dalton's solid spheres (1803) gave way to Thomson's plum pudding (1897) when the electron was found. Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment (1911) showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with mostly empty space around it. Bohr (1913) put electrons in shells at fixed distances, and Chadwick (1932) found the neutron in the nucleus.

kid: No one can see inside an atom. So scientists build a model: a picture that fits the evidence. When a new test does not fit, the model has to change. The model of the atom changed four times in about 130 years.

In 1803 John Dalton said atoms were tiny solid spheres. Then in 1897 J. J. Thomson found the electron, a tiny negative particle much lighter than any atom. So atoms had parts inside. His plum pudding model was a ball of positive charge with electrons dotted through it.

Rutherford's team fired positive alpha particles at thin gold foil. If the pudding model was right, they should all go almost straight through. Most did. But a few swung off course, and about 1 in 8000 bounced back. So the positive charge and nearly all the mass must sit in a tiny centre: the nucleus. The rest of the atom is mostly empty space. This is the nuclear model.

Niels Bohr then showed that electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances, called shells or energy levels. This explained why atoms give out light of only certain colours. Later work showed the positive charge comes from protons. In 1932 James Chadwick found the neutron, a neutral particle in the nucleus. That gives the model you use today.
adult: This is GCSE content: AQA Combined Science 4.1.1.3, with matching OCR and Edexcel content. Students must say why the plum pudding model gave way to the nuclear model, and what Bohr and Chadwick added. It is also a core example of Working Scientifically. Each new model came from evidence the old one could not explain.

The key experiment is alpha particle scattering. Geiger and Marsden ran it under Rutherford from 1909, and he explained it in 1911. Thinly spread positive charge cannot turn a fast alpha particle much. The few large turns and rare bounces need a concentrated positive charge. Its push grows fast as the particle gets closer.

Common mistakes: saying alpha particles passed through gaps between atoms, not through the atoms; thinking electrons deflected them (they are about 8000 times lighter); muddling the order of the models; saying Bohr found the neutron; and treating old models as foolish, when each fitted the evidence of its time.

In the lab, students order the five models on a timeline. They fire alpha particles at gold foil with real inverse-square repulsion, then aim at one zoomed-in nucleus until a particle bounces back. Last, they match six pieces of evidence to the change each one forced.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to explain the gold foil result as a story: what Rutherford expected, what he saw, and why that meant a nucleus. Then ask why a model that later turns out wrong can still be good science.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: order the atom models, fire alpha particles at gold foil, aim one at a nucleus to bounce it back, and match evidence to each change.

practice.prompt: Which discovery showed that atoms are not solid spheres that cannot be split?
practice.hint: Which discovery came first, and showed a part inside atoms?
practice.explain: In 1897 Thomson found the electron, a particle smaller than an atom. So atoms have parts inside, and he proposed the plum pudding model.

practice.prompt: About 1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced back. Roughly how many thousand alpha particles must be fired to see {b} bounce back?
practice.hint: Each bounce needs about 8 thousand particles.
practice.explain: 1 in 8000 means about 8 thousand per bounce, so {b} bounces need about {=8*b} thousand alpha particles.

practice.prompt: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?
choices: Most of the atom is empty space
There are gaps between the gold atoms
Alpha particles are too small to hit anything
practice.hint: The foil is many atoms thick. What is inside each atom?
practice.explain: The particles went through the atoms themselves. Almost all of each atom is empty space around a tiny nucleus.

practice.prompt: An atom is about 100,000 times wider than its nucleus. If a model nucleus were a {a} cm marble, how many km wide would the model atom be?
practice.hint: Multiply by 100,000 to get cm. 100,000 cm is 1 km.
practice.explain: {a} cm × 100,000 = {a} km. Almost all of that is empty space.

pool.prompt: What did the plum pudding model predict for the gold foil experiment?
choices: Nearly all alpha particles pass almost straight through
pool.hint: In the pudding, positive charge is spread thinly.
pool.explain: Thinly spread charge is too weak to deflect a fast alpha particle much, so the model predicted almost no deflection.

pool.prompt: A few alpha particles bounced back. What did this show?
choices: Positive charge and mass are packed in a tiny nucleus
pool.hint: What could push a fast, positive particle right back?
pool.explain: Only a concentrated positive charge with most of the mass can repel an alpha particle that strongly.

pool.prompt: What did Bohr add to the nuclear model?
choices: Electrons orbit in shells at fixed distances
pool.hint: His idea explained the exact colours of light atoms give out.
pool.explain: Bohr put electrons in shells (energy levels) at fixed distances from the nucleus.

choices: Solid sphere, plum pudding, nuclear, shells
Plum pudding, solid sphere, shells, nuclear
Nuclear, plum pudding, solid sphere, shells
pool.hint: Dalton came first, and Bohr built on Rutherford.
pool.explain: Dalton 1803, Thomson 1897, Rutherford 1911, Bohr 1913, with Chadwick's neutron in 1932.

choices: The neutron, a neutral particle in the nucleus
pool.hint: It was found in 1932 and has no charge.
pool.explain: Chadwick found the neutron, which explained why nuclei have more mass than their protons alone.

pool.prompt: Why was the plum pudding model replaced?
choices: The alpha scattering results did not fit it
pool.hint: What makes scientists change a model?
pool.explain: A model changes when new evidence does not fit it. The scattering results needed a nucleus.

pool.prompt: In a simulation, {a} alpha particles are fired and {b} are deflected. How many go straight through?
pool.hint: Take the deflected ones away from the total.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} pass straight through, which is most of them.

pool.prompt: A helium nucleus has 2 protons but a mass of 4. A nucleus has {a} protons and a mass of {b}. How many neutrons does it have?
pool.hint: Neutrons make up the mass that protons do not.
pool.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a} neutrons. Chadwick's neutron explained this missing mass.

pool.prompt: Why could electrons not have caused the big deflections?
choices: They are about 8000 times lighter than an alpha particle
pool.hint: Think about mass: can a light thing turn a heavy one round?
pool.explain: Electrons are far too light to turn a heavy alpha particle round. The deflections came from the nucleus.
